newsitem.title: UK: Further BA discounting feature of ex-UK air.
newsitem.headline: Further BA discounting feature of ex-UK air.

text.p: The Far East has been one of the healthier spots in the ex-UK market air cargo market where discounting by British Airways has been a key factor, a Reuters survey showed.
At the same time, many other airlines are weighing a rates increase in early spring of five to 10 percent.

The only Far Eastern destination to be subject to the BA campaign which lasts until March two is Beijing but special pallet rates are being offered to the Middle East and the Indian sub-continent as well as in Europe and particularly on the North Atlantic where discounts are available on 25 routes.

BA confirmed it is offering special promotional type 5 pallet rates on a total of 53 route spread over the North Atlantic, Europe ,BA's southern region comprising the Middle East, East Africa and the Indian sub-continent as well as Beijing.
As was the case in January the promotion allows forwarders to heavily undercut other carriers and to still make money even if the pallets are not full, industry sources said.
In January discounts were as much as one third with transatlantic rates attracting most attention.
Most other carriers reckon BA is only able fill its planes at a seasonally quiet time of year by cutting rates to a level which cannot cover costs.

On February 6, BA World Cargo's managing director, Kevin Hatton when asked by Reuters about discounting said: " We will do what is right for the business. We want to improve the bottom line. We'll do what is most effective."

However in sharp contrast other airlines are talking in terms of rate increases in the next few months if not actually announcing them. They are hoping that rates can be lifted by between five and ten percent at the start of April - a traditional time for lifting rates with the introduction of summer timetables.

They said they would aim for a rates increase that would be separate from existing fuel surcharges as the latter should remain in force as long as kerosene prices stay some 30 percent above those of last summer.

Air France UK cargo manager Anne Veyssie said the surcharge does not cover fully increased fuel costs -- a view shared with several other carriers who said they did not want to see the surcharge absorbed into rates which would then have to unscrambled if and when energy prices fell.

Cathay Pacific's Ivor Llewellyn said it might try and drop flat surcharges and replace them different ones for different destinations which would be a fairer way of charging for the increased fuel costs.
"We're looking for increases from April of six to ten percent," he added.
Some carriers said a number of the other major national west European carriers were also cutting ex-UK rates to combat BA's promotion which had been depressing rates to the Mideast gulf.
But several overseas carriers said that ex-UK cargo demand was standing up well and is much more buoyant than exports from continental Europe.

For example the airlines said that exports to the Far East from Germany and Italy were fairly sluggish resulting in European carriers cutting rates for ex-UK cargo in order to attract busines to freighters flying eastwards from Europe. Any such cargo would first be trucked to Europe.
Last year's surge in exports to China has fallen back following, the imposition of an import tax aimed slowing economic activity, airline officials said.
Korean Air cargo sales manager Frank Smith said the ex-UK market to South Korea and Japan has generally been fairly quiet although he has been able to fly most planes with reasonable capacity.
Last year the UK was one of the few KAL stations to beat its targets and was only bettered by the U.S., he added. Milan and Amsterdam just met targets but others lagged.
At times in late 1996 some of KAL's ex-UK traffic had to be trucked to Frankfurt because of pressure on capacity on direct flights.

One unusual cargo coming up for KAL is a 747 charter from Shannon to Korea which will carry 86 horses -three to a pallet - at the end of April, Smith stated. KAL has had other enquiries for carrying Irish horses whose popularity has grown as they are seen as better value than English ones.
Another business which is getting under way again is in live day-old chicks to the Far East.

The amount of cargo heading eastwards has been highlighted by general sales agent (GSA) Air Cargo Trader getting near regular weekly service with an Aeroflot Ilyushin Il-76 freighter which will take high tech computer and telecommunication parts from Ireland to Japan flying from Shannon via Moscow and Novosibirsk.

Although running with capacity at reasonable levels, Air New Zealand's Phil Rawlings said it has slowed with bookings now only a couple days ahead of departure compared with the pre-Christmas rush when planes were booked a week before take-off.
Air Canada's Mike Judkins said it flew general consolidated cargo to New Delhi which is mainly loaded in London on a 747 combi flying in from Vancouver.
Emirates cargo sales manager in London Roy Disson said the airline would not be trying to match BA's ex-UK to tthe Middle East ratessaying its emphasis is on "keeping yields up".

The size of BA's discounts is not reflected in the rates table accompanying this report as they are not really available for small shipments of 100 kilos but need to be at least 500 kilos, other carriers said. - Reuters Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44 171 542 7706 Fax:5017
